utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. We have a late start, both because Mr. Krajisnik had to go to the dentist and for technical problems, computers. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, I was informed that there will be a follow-up dentist appointment next week. We are sitting in the afternoon, so therefore if that's in the morning, it does not in any way interfere with the court sessions. That's one. Then second, you have provided the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I, just on that subject --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I haven't spoken directly to Mr. Krajisnik. I gathered that he had a relatively major piece of dentistry carried out to his mouth this morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we start the examination I certainly would have asked Mr. Krajisnik whether the consequences of it could have been that he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't forget that. There's another matter. For sure by now 12 exhibits have not been assigned a number, and I invited the registrar to keep a list and then to assign numbers. That list is not yet ready. Nevertheless, we'll continue today numbering exhibits with 12 numbers in between. There might be 13th or a 14th or a 15th, and then that would not be a chronological order. That's then a pity, but that is something we can live with. So at this moment, 12 numbers will be kept open for that list and then we'll continue. Mr. Krajisnik, before we resume the -- the examination -- the cross-examination, I'd like to be informed on whether the treatment this morning by the dentist would have influenced your -- your abilities to concentrate on questions, to answer questions. I can imagine that some anaesthetics were, for example, applied, and whether you yourself have any indication that you would not be fully able to testify in this court, could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was suggested by my legal officer whether this should be done in private session. I don't think that this is such a personal matter. I mean, anaesthetics have their effect or do not have any effect. So I'd just like to know from you whether you feel comfortable in continuing or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to continue the examination. If you're asking whether I have a tooth ache, well, yes, I do. It's quite a tooth ache; my nerve was extracted. But I would like to continue this examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please feel free, and please even accept that the Chamber would appreciate that if at any moment you feel that this tooth ache would negatively -- have a negative impact on your ability to testify, please tell us immediately because we don't want to take any risk in this respect. Then, Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps not a surprise, I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony and I'll invite Mr. Tieger to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, yesterday we reviewed a number of telephone conversations involving Mr. Cizmovic and Dr. Karadzic, and I was about to present you with one more when the session adjourned yesterday. I'd like to do that now. That's found at tab 71 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, that's not correct. Tab 75. And I believe this will need an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1192, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, P1192, as I mentioned, is a conversation between Mr. Cizmovic and Dr. Karadzic on March 1st, 1992. And, Mr. Krajisnik, if we can look first at the middle part of the first --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please read it? May I? I've never seen this before. May I read this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course. And before you review it - and I hope quickly - let me -- Mr. Krajisnik, I was going to mention that I'll be bringing your attention to about the tenth line down the first page, Mr. Cizmovic talking about people calling him a leg-man or, I think in that context, meaning an errand boy, something to that effect, and continuing on for about ten lines, and I'll also be turning your attention to the last line of that conversation where Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Cizmovic talk about his position. Those --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Court, those passages are found in the middle part of page 1, the top part of page 2, and the first half of page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While Mr. Krajisnik's -- Krajisnik reads it, I must admit that the word "leg-man" is not familiar to me and it is repeated several times. Could someone explain to me what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Gopher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which brings me another word. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I make this suggestion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- that Your Honour ask Mr. Krajisnik what he understands that term to be in his language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In other words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I then, of course, have to identify the word in B/C/S, which is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: "Potrckalo" in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Potrckalo," Mr. Krajisnik; could you tell me what that is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Potrckalo," in Serbian, Bosnian, and Croatian means someone who is a lackey. When you tell them: Run off, do something, "lackey" would be the best word. That's a person who does whatever you ask him to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I can see you're reviewing this conversation with considerable -- in considerable detail and with a great detail of scrutiny. It may be more helpful if I direct you to -- if you review it enough to be familiar with its general contents and then I then direct you to the particular portions of interest which I already indicated to you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I'm about to finish. Sorry, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next time --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- even if there is a long conversation you have not read before, we'll allow Mr. Tieger to put a question, and if it appears reasonable that you would have to read the context in order to answer that question, you certainly will be given an opportunity to do so, but it's also imaginable that he's asking explanation of one specific word used where it's less important. So next time, Mr. Tieger, you may put a question to Mr. Krajisnik, and if there's any need for Mr. Krajisnik to read the context, whether it's reasonable, then of course we'll allow him to do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, as appears from the conversation, it seems that Mr. Cizmovic at this point is expressing some concern about the way he's being depicted by others. The question was asked about the meaning of that particular word and we find it in the early part of the conversation when Mr. Cizmovic says: "Well people are calling me, they tell me I'm a leg-man -" which we've also heard as gopher and which you've explained as lackey - "and many other things." The conversation goes on: "What kind of a friend is that, what kind of a leader is that who is calling his Government coordinator a leg-man? Is his absolutism so ...?" And Dr. Karadzic, as he does through the conversation, tries to reassure him. He says: "Ah, fuck them. They want ... it's clear what they want ..." et cetera. It continues on the next page, where Dr. Karadzic makes reference to: "We'll quiet things down. If they print something like that, I'll do something to fuck them up." And then Mr. Cizmovic says: "... I know all the contents outside. But I simply believe that I wasn't a leg-man, and I didn't accept to work as a leg-man. I accepted to do what I could do."

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC SAYS
utterances.text: "We are all leg-men for the Serbian people and you can say that freely, we're all leg-men for Serbian people. We are not leg-men for any party or any personality but for Serbian people. We are all rushing to do this, and we could all do something else." And then I indicated earlier I would turn your attention also to the last part of the conversation which appears at the first half of page 3, and the third page of the intercept for you as well, Mr. Krajisnik, in the B/C/S. Karadzic: "I'm telling you, tell me how you would like to define it, and we'll define it as you wish, considering that, that ..." Cizmovic: "What, what was I now until now?" Karadzic: "So far you were the coordinator of the Ministry Council for the relation with municipalities. It was a very ..." Cizmovic: "With the governments?" Karadzic: "Yes." Cizmovic: "I think that it's the third-highest position in Republika Srpska." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, when Mr. Cizmovic tells Dr. Karadzic that in his view the position Mr. Cizmovic holds is the third-highest position in Republika Srpska, can you assist us in identifying who he would have meant as the two positions higher than his or the two persons who were his superiors?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could just guess, but this is a conversation where he promotes himself to high office. He wants to become Prime Minister of the future government. At least, that's my reading of it. How could he possibly be the number three person when there is a president of the Council of Ministers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you asked whether Mr. Krajisnik would assist us in identifying who he would have meant. Mr. Krajisnik started his answer by saying: "I can only guess." Guessing does not assist. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept that. However, sometimes that's simply a turn of phrase intended to mean the person can't precisely know what is in the mind of the person but then proceeds to provide information that assists the Court in identifying, and I think that may be what Mr. Krajisnik was attempting to do at that point, but I will be alert to those clues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber finds it useless to continue these kind of guessing exercises or speculations. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you know to whom Mr. Cizmovic reported during 1992 -- the latter part of 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. Maybe there are some reports that you could give me and then I can give you my comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn next then to the 6th Session of the Assembly of the Serbian People held on January 26th, 1992. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, this was an extraordinary session of the Assembly of the Serbian People, as is reflected in your introductory remarks on the first page. And on the agenda, as you indicate, there was one item. "Analysis of the proceedings of the 9th Session of the Bosnian Assembly, including the measures and decisions taken." And then a discussion of that issue results. I'm not interested in the specific details of the conduct of the session -- of the 9th Session of the Bosnian Assembly, but in essence, Mr. Krajisnik, was it the case that that was another step forward in the movement of the Muslim side toward the independence of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And let's -- a bit more specifically, that was a movement toward the holding of the referendum that could lead to the -- to recognition by the European Community and independence. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe this has been misinterpreted. A decision was passed, that is to say an unconstitutional decision, on a referendum on independence for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was done by the Muslim representatives. That is the last session that I presided over, even after the veto of the Serb side. The interpretation I heard was "initiative." It was not an initiative; it was a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in response to that, a special and extraordinary session of the Assembly of the Serbian People was called to review what had happened and determine what should be done in response?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I don't know how well you recall that particular session by memory so, if necessary, I'll be happy to direct your attention to particular portions. But is it fair to say, in your view, that various deputies were calling for measures to be taken, for action to be taken, for progress to be made toward the completion of tasks necessary to define Serbian ethnic territory and establish organs in those territories?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please be given the possibility to explain later? And now I want to say something else to you. It's not only that. There were all sorts of proposals there, very radical proposals, if you are referring to the Assembly of the Serb People. But I ask and request that I explain why this was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, is this information you'd like to receive from Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The why --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I wasn't directing my attention to the why at this point. It may be relevant during the course of other questions, and in that case Mr. Krajisnik could be in a position to provide that information, but no, it's not necessary to move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're first interested in what rather than why it happened, so then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did not say if Mr. Tieger wishes this to be done; I am asking, requesting, that I be given an opportunity to explain because you've always allowed me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Tieger is limited in his time. I allowed you to add anything at the end of your testimony. Mr. Tieger at this moment is seeking answers to a question on what happened during that session, and at this moment rather wants to spend time on that than on explanations why things happened. If this is of great relevance, perhaps in re-examination Mr. Josse will re-visit these matters. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, irrespective, Mr. Krajisnik, of the precise nature of the suggestions made by the deputies, however radical they may have been and the range of suggestions that may have been made - and all that information is available to the Court - in the Assembly session, that's what people were talking about; what to do in response to the actions taken at the 9th Session of the Bosnian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cizmovic, as we've heard before, also spoke at that session and spoke relatively early, at page 13 of the English -- actually, before I get to his comments, let me note that he spoke just after Mr. Vjestica and Mr. Novakovic. Mr. Vjestica spoke at the beginning of page 10 of the English and at SA025256 of your version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, yesterday it was minus one, today it's plus one. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's probably not precisely the kind of balance the Court would like me to strike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just for the record that people can -- are able to find it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vjestica indicated he wanted to be as brief and to the point as possible, spoke initially about the need to adopt the already-mentioned constitution, and then continued at the fifth paragraph about the need for representatives and commissions of autonomous regions to work simultaneously with the commissions in Sarajevo on the preparation of all documents of the autonomous regions so that laws can be adopted, and then continued on to the top of page 11 in the English - and I think still on page 5256 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik - "All these duties are immense because we are setting up our own state. In carrying them out, there must be a great deal of discipline, hard work and respect for, if I can call it like that, the centre." He goes on to propose the need for deadlines, suggesting the 15th of April [sic], because the work is extensive, and states that: "The operative plan should be drawn up to define tasks precisely, those charged with executing them, and the deadlines for their completion. People to whom these tasks are to be assigned should openly say if they can carry them out. Those who feel unable, should say so now and allow us to select those who can." Sorry, and I read the 15th of April, I believe the text says, and I -- the 15th of February. So, Mr. Krajisnik, is it fair to say that at an early stage of this session, in response to that single agenda item, the discussion became quite concrete?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, people presented various specific proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I had indicated that Mr. Cizmovic then spoke shortly after Mr. Vjestica, and he began his comments by saying: "Esteemed President, ladies and gentlemen. "In respect of the proposal that has been submitted and which was to be scheduled to be decided upon now, I would like to point out there is something that implies dynamics."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Too fast, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He then goes on to mention the Council of Ministers and the need for the council to submit a programme and deadlines for completion of tasks. "These deadlines should be met." So like Mr. Vjestica, Mr. Cizmovic is also being concrete in his suggestions to those assembled about what response should be taken?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know because I haven't read it. I believe so, but I would have to read what he said, and I believe he did speak about specific proposals, although this doesn't look like a specific proposal concerning borders, but he must have spoken in the same vein as the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then about six paragraphs from when he begins, on page 13 of the English and SA025260 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Vjestica says - and this is something that was read out to you by Mr. Stewart during the course of your examination-in-chief -- Mr. Cizmovic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CIZMOVIC SAYS
utterances.text: "To solve this problem, I propose that we begin with an urgent operationalisation and a declaration on the establishment and promulgation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Tasks set out in the instructions of 19 December, 1991, should be carried out."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just tell me where that is. I haven't found that particular passage, although -- yes, I found it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, as we can see, Mr. Vjestica -- Mr. Cizmovic not only makes explicit reference to the Variant A and B instructions, but states that: "The fulfilment of those instructions is precisely what is required to move forward toward the establishment of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and to respond to the -- to what you call the illegal actions taken by the Bosnian Assembly at the 9th Session. You said during the course of your direct examination, Mr. Krajisnik, that you didn't pay attention to this reference or you didn't note the reference because Mr. Cizmovic was -- because you were paying attention to the main topic, or you were only paying attention that day to the main topic of discussion. Isn't it the case, Mr. Krajisnik, that Mr. Cizmovic was directing his attention -- his remarks were all about the main topic of discussion that day?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of those points made by Cizmovic are contained there. I didn't notice that he mentioned instructions. He referred to the declaration about establishment. There's nothing about A and B, and it does say "19th December," though, which seems to justify your theory. But at that moment, I really didn't pay attention to that. Just point me to one thing that has to do with the instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, when Mr. Cizmovic referred to himself as occupying the third-most important position in Republika Srpska at that time as coordinator of the autonomous regions for the Ministerial Council, you seem to indicate that you didn't think that was the case and that he was angling for an even more important position than he held. But is it fair to say that the person who was tasked with responsibility to go from municipality to municipality to ensure that the objectives of Dr. Karadzic and the Ministerial Council were fulfilled was perceived by the persons in those municipalities as having an important function?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Prosecutor. We had Neskovic who had the same job. There were hundreds of representatives of Mr. Karadzic like that whom he sent into the field, and he's a member of the Ministerial Council. He was coordinator of autonomous regions. In the Ministerial Council, he was just a member. The Ministerial Council had its president, but he was blowing his own horn, trying to make himself seem more important than he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'll remind you that we've seen the minutes of the 2nd Session of that Assembly where concern was expressed about the pace at which the conclusions of the first meeting were being fulfilled and that Mr. Cizmovic was charged with what had to be seen by the Ministerial Council and by you and Dr. Karadzic, who attended that session, as being an important task.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- what I understood I said at the session and you didn't let me read it. There need to be a -- there needs to be a distinction between what the Ministerial Council is doing, the government, and the Assembly. Find it, find the relevant Assembly session. Cizmovic is an excellent lawyer, but I don't see why this would be an important post that he held. That's what I said and that's my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you say "there needs to be a distinction between the Ministerial Council -- between what the Ministerial Council is doing, the government, and the Assembly," are you there -- did you use the term "government" there as a synonym for Ministerial Council, or were you suggesting that the Ministerial Council, the government, and the Assembly were all separate organs at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it says there what is written in Serbian, I said that a distinction needs to be made between what the Assembly is doing, the Ministerial Council, and the party, meaning the SDS. I don't think "government" is written there. That's my -- from my memory. I don't have the background material in front of me. So between the Ministerial Council, the party, and the Assembly - "party" meaning SDS. I wanted basically everyone to do their own job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask there one question just in between. Mr. Krajisnik, it -- I understood your last answer to be that party, Assembly -- they all had their own responsibilities. At the same time, what seems to have been a party document, that is the 19th of December instructions, were discussed and introduced as -- not only once. If at least we would accept that this is a reference to the A and B variant document are discussed at non-party sessions because the Assembly sessions were not party sessions but were Assembly sessions, which gives the impression, at first sight, that party matters and Assembly matters would not always clearly be separated. Could you assist me in whether I did perceive this in the right way or whether I should look at it from a different point of view. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Mr. President, I remember that it was just mentioned. I don't remember the instructions A and B were ever discussed at the Assembly. But you're right. Very often people tried to impinge on other people's responsibilities, and that's why I wanted to strictly divide jurisdictions. I wanted everyone to do their own job. So if that was the job of the party, the responsibility of the party, then let the party do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but here again, Mr. Krajisnik, we have a -- a little problem. We do not read here that you say: That's a party matter, I don't even know what you're talking about, so let's keep it out. Your answer now says: It should have been separated. That's not what we read at that time. So therefore, we are trying to establish what actually happened at that moment, and of course sometimes your present views on the matter assist us in understanding it, but of course it could not replace what happened at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was talking about the meeting of the Ministerial Council, and there I said that jurisdictions should be divided, that we should know who is doing what at the 2nd Session, whereas here, if you want to know why I didn't react, I can explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could do it briefly, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very simple. I probably understood the first sentence that -- about the declaration on establishment and proclamation of the Serb Republic. That was clear. That was our responsibility. As for these instructions, I'm not going to claim they didn't exist, I don't know whether they existed. But I didn't -- it didn't stick in my memory. I didn't remember that, although it may have been distributed right in front of me. I'm not denying they existed. Maybe they did exist, maybe somebody was handing them out standing right next to me. But it was never the subject of discussion at an Assembly session. It was never the subject of division of activities. If you see this contribution recorded here, then it must have been said, but I never dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you may have missed the point, but where you say it has never been the subject of discussion, Mr. Cizmovic makes proposals on the basis of these instructions, whether or not it was followed up, et cetera. But to that extent, it has been introduced during this Assembly meeting, at least if the reference is to the Variant A and B document. But let's not further discuss that. But I'm just pointing at what seems, on the basis of these minutes, to be a fact. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you said that these instructions were never the subject of discussion at an Assembly session. The next Assembly session after the 6th Session, that we've just been looking at, was the session held on February 15th; and the day before there was a meeting which was an extended session of the main and Executive Boards of the SDS and the Deputies' Club on 14 February. And we can find that located at tab 70. And at page 5 of the English and page 04002200 of the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- Dr. Karadzic says: "Now it seems to me, and that is also the opinion of Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Krajisnik" --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just find that passage. Could you point me to the line so I can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's about eight lines down from the top, and you'll probably easily find the names Koljevic -- it says Koljevica and Krajisnika.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And again, quoting Dr. Karadzic: "Now it seems to me, and that is also the opinion of Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Krajisnik, that now it would be more important to gain the real situation, the factual situation on the ground." Then he continues, about eight lines down: "Now that the main attitude towards Yugoslavia during this entire interfering of the European Community was that the Serbs were right, but that the factual situation was so-and-so. Now we are in the position to say - yes, maybe the Muslims are right, but the factual situation is so-and-so, although they are not right. The factual situation is so-and-so, now it is so, now it's up to us. It's up to each individual to do his part of the job." And as we've seen, Mr. Krajisnik, at -- in earlier parts of the case, Dr. Karadzic then goes on to make four separate references to the initiation of stage number 2. And I can direct your attention to those specifically, but I suspect that you may recall having seen those and heard those during the course of this case. But I'm happy to do so otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Court, those are located at pages 5 through 6 of the English, page 7, page 17, and page 24.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me where it is for me. I have this 220 page. But it doesn't matter. If you -- if you say that is so, I can just comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I directed your attention to those, Mr. Krajisnik, as you recall, in response to your comment that this was never discussed at an Assembly session. And while this is not an Assembly session, it's a meeting attended by those people who are present at Assembly sessions.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic says here that factual situation should be taken over, because we didn't have power where we had won it. That's one. It says also that we have to be just towards Croats and Muslims, that nobody should run away from our territories. And then it also goes on - and you're right - that it says we should control access to our areas. That's the 25th of February. And as for what you say about degree 1 and 2, just after that I see it was mentioned, that is at the club of deputies. I don't believe it was mentioned at an Assembly session. I'm not saying I never heard it; maybe I did hear it. But I just understood from all of it that we should take control where we had not done so yet. But I -- I mean, I really don't rule out that Variants A and B existed. Right here I didn't understand it that way. I saw what the reasons were. I understood them. And this was mainly a discussion about the reasons and about what needed to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And how it was to be accomplished. On page 24 of the English and page 22 -- 2214 of your version, Dr. Karadzic says -- I'll give you a chance to find that. It's at the very top of the B/C/S. And the -- about the top one -- about the bottom third of page 24 in the English.

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC SAYS
utterances.text: "That is why we called you today, to intensify, to introduce the second level, and to intensify the functioning of the government at any cost and on every single millimetre of our territory."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what's written here indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's how the intensification of the process of moving forward on every single millimetre of our territory, as Dr. Karadzic put it, was to move forward, by introducing the second level.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what was supposed to be raised into -- it says: "to enhance the functioning of authorities in every part of our areas," if that's what you mean. I understood that. And in another passage he said instructions would be given, but instructions were not given here. He just said the functioning of authorities should be enhanced in every part of our areas. I didn't hear about instructions. I heard about this bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you also heard about introducing the second level. Dr. Karadzic clearly, I think it's fair to say, was directing himself to assemble people who knew what the second level was when he made four separate references to it. Is it your testimony that you're the only person there who didn't know what the second level meant?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the only person. Everybody whom you had brought here, everybody whom I had talked to, they don't remember this. And believe me when I say I don't remember about it. I don't know what the second degree or second level is. And it's not a preparation. Preparations were being made for a state of war, but this was the 25th of February. I'm not saying I didn't hear this, but I thought it had to do with the functioning of the authorities and I understood that instructions would be given. I assure you that I understand what he is saying, not the second level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, when you referred to the 25th of February, from what I remember, it was the 14th of February, just to avoid any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, sorry. It was the 25th of February a moment ago. We are now talking about the 14th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there were negotiations going on then about the Cutileiro Plan. I don't know what this is. This is after the referendum, or maybe before the referendum was held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you have several times put it to Mr. Krajisnik that, in your view, reference was made to the 19th of December instructions, the Variant A and B instructions. Mr. Krajisnik has said several times that he didn't know them at the time, and that to the extent he heard these observations, that he never linked them to anything that was familiar to him at that moment. You could go on with that for ages --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I apologise if I gave the impression I was about to ask that question again; I was about to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. But I don't know what other references there will be, but if there will be at any moment any reference to it which Mr. Krajisnik would have understood otherwise, he'll certainly tell us. And if Mr. Krajisnik did not make that link, of course the Chamber not on the subjective understanding of what was said by Mr. Krajisnik but on the objective analysis of the evidence we have will see whether any inference can be drawn from these texts. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the next day was the 7th Session of the Assembly of the Serbian People. That's February 15th. Mr. Stewart brought that session to your attention during the course of your examination-in-chief. And in particular, he directed your attention to remarks by Dr. Kalinic, found at page 54 of the English. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, even without a plus one or minus one rule, I cannot find Mr. Kalinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe page 57 of the English, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I missed -- as a matter of fact, I missed the word "Dr. Kalinic" on the top of page 54. I apologise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A lot of numbers were mentioned, Mr. Krajisnik. The last was page 57 for your benefit. Do you see Dr. Kalinic's remarks there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the remarks in particular were: "Earlier today" -- "Earlier today, in a smaller group, I suggested a medical procedure. You know that our ministers, our Council of Ministers with Mr. Cizmovic and Mr. Simovic, are to tour all our municipalities and establish the true situation during the next seven days, which would help us determine whether we have an infrastructure which may become operational once we proclaim our Serbian Republic or not. We cannot be sovereign if we are not able to extra power over the territory that is ours."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 58 is the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you indicated in response to Mr. Stewart's questions that you don't know what smaller group Dr. Kalinic was referring to and, essentially, as I understood it correctly, knew nothing in particular about this suggestion by Dr. Kalinic. If I'm wrong about that, please correct me. And if you do know something about it, please tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he talked to me at all, whether I was there, who -- I don't know who this small group is. I'm not precluding this possibility. I mean, I am not precluding the possibility that I was in that group, but I don't know what group that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, if you could turn to page 59 of the English and page -- I think it will be 62 of your version. That's Dr. Karadzic speaking. And he says at the top of page 59 in the English: "I'm asking our coordinator and the president of the Council of Ministers, Mr. Simovic, to hold briefings with municipal presidents and other participants, or representatives in governments and regional Assemblies. What Mr. Kalinic has said is very important. We should have a questionnaire which could be utilised to check our particular segments of the infrastructure on the ground. Then we shall have our coordinator of the Council of Ministers, Mr. Cizmovic, spend the next week on wheels, first paying visits to the regional centres, in Trebinje, Bijeljina, Doboj, Banja Luka and with us here in Sarajevo, and then going to the smaller towns, in order to establish, or perhaps authorise someone else in each municipality to do that, on the basis of a questionnaire with ten or 15 basic questions, to establish how elements of the authorities really work, for instance the SUP, to see if there is any loyalty out there," et cetera. He goes on to talk about people in the municipalities who are not loyal. "Check out the SDK," et cetera. And then finally concludes: "If we could afford to spend some time compiling a questionnaire which would be used for a check-up and a reminder to those municipalities who have not taken care of all the preparations that they must do so. I suggest that we meet later in Mr. Krajisnik's conference room. That is all from me." Mr. Krajisnik, does that assist you now in recalling what Dr. Karadzic described as "very important," that is the need to have Mr. Cizmovic at that time spend the week going to as many regional centres as possible with a questionnaire designed to assist in determining the state of preparation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any of this, but I'm connecting this to the telephone conversation that you showed me here, that Cizmovic said there was this questionnaire. But this is all right, as far as I'm concerned, if we're going to promulgate a constitution, whether the government is actually functioning in the areas where we are in power. Mr. Cizmovic was supposed to be there only up to the New Year on the basis of that conversation, but I see now that he went on. It was probably Mr. Karadzic's decision, based on some need for him to go on working. I'd just like to remind you of something else: Very soon the Ministerial Council was abolished and a government was elected soon after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have two final matters I want to bring to your attention in connection with the Variant A and B document, Mr. Krajisnik. First is found at tab 72, and it's a decision on the proclamation of the Serbian Assembly of Ilidza municipality from January 3rd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's P529, tab 53, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, as we can see at the top of this document, Mr. Krajisnik, it states, among -- it says: "Pursuant to Article 265, of the SRBiH Constitution and will of the Serbian people from the territory of Ilidza, expressed at the plebiscite held on 9 and 10 November, 1991, and according to the instructions given by the BiH Serbian Democratic Party (Main Board), number: 079 from 19 December, 1991, of Assembly of Serbian People Ilidza at the session held on January 3rd have reached -- 1992, have reached the following decision." Then, Mr. Krajisnik, if we turn to the second page of the document and look to the bottom we can see the persons to whom this decision was submitted. And at the very top of that list we can see that it was submitted to you, the president of the Serbian Assembly of BiH.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 3rd of January, when I was president of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know whether I got it or not. Maybe it went to the party, but if you remember my response in relation to this document -- well, I can repeat it again now: I did not have any coordination with them because they passed a decision, they founded a Presidency towards the end of 1992 on the basis of a document passed by the Assembly that such bodies were being abolished. And this was December, 1992. They established a Presidency on the basis of the decision whereby Presidencies and commissioners were abolished. I don't know how it could have gone to Bosnia-Herzegovina -- or rather, the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Maybe it went to the party, or maybe it reached someone; not that it reached me. It shouldn't have been sent to me in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid, Mr. Krajisnik, I'm having a great deal of difficulty following your response. I'm not quite sure what the establishment of a Presidency toward the end of 1992, in December of 1992, has with your receipt of a submitted document in January of 1992, nor can I understand what the fact that you occupied both the position of president of the Assembly of the BiH government and the president of the -- sorry, Assembly, and the president of the Assembly of the Serbian People would have any impact on the receipt of a document clearly submitted to the president of the Serbian Assembly of BiH.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll explain it to you now, Mr. Prosecutor. I'm telling you that I did not have any contact with them. Had I had contact with them, he would have said on the basis of the recommendation of the Assembly of the Serb People, I establish such and such. There was this recommendation in December, and I could have said to them: This is the recommendation and establish an Assembly on the basis of that, if you wish. The -- my office was in the office of the president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, although I was president of the Serb Assembly. And I'm -- that was in January. And I did not have any communication with them, and I'm giving you this example that towards the end of the year, on the basis of some document that abolishes Presidencies and commissioners, they are establishing a Presidency of Ilidza. And I would say to them: Well, look, you have this recommendation here. Why are you establishing a body which is not necessary? There is this recommendation. And this recommendation, in terms of establishing an Assembly of the Serb People, was passed only 20 days before that. So had I had contact with them, that is what I would have suggested. And that was the only legal channel, as established by the Assembly, through the recommendation, not this way. Because if the Assembly had this recommendation, they would not have adopted this. They would have said: You have this particular instruction, and that's it, whereas these people were a minority. This is for Variant B. So they were a minority. They did not have a majority in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Krajisnik, in connection with a number of assertions you made, including any discussion about this document at an Assembly, I'd like you to turn, please, to tab 73, which contain --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This will need a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1193, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which contain remarks from the tape-recording of the 33rd Session of the Republika Srpska National Assembly held on the 20th and the 21st of July, 1993. And in the first page of both the English and B/C/S extracts, we can see the remarks of the municipality president of Jajce, which begins by addressing you, Mr. Krajisnik: "Mr. Chairman, gentlemen, deputies, and dear guests," saying: "We already have what Mr. Chairman was talking about." And then he goes on in the second paragraph: "If we go back a little and recall the material that was coming from the Main Board as activities in the field, and there were two options: Variant A -- or a) variant and b) variant. Variant a) is for the municipalities with the majority of Serbs; variant b) for municipalities where they are not a majority, as in Jajce. Then we established the Municipal Assembly according to these instructions, and later on municipal organs of authority. That was all done before the war, actually, on 27 January, 1992. We held the constituent session of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Jajce where a decision regarding merging with the Autonomous Region of Krajina was made and a request was sent to the National Assembly, actually, it was then the Assembly of the Serbian People of BiH, to carry out verification and I think the verification was done at the end of February." Then he goes on in the next paragraph, in the second sentence -- in the third sentence of that paragraph: "And when we were to establish a Serbian municipality of Jajce according to the instructions, in accordance with the order issued by Mr. Karadzic and your order, I conducted talks with all the committee members in the joint Assembly, who were Serbs, and only one of them agreed to enter the joint, that is Serbian Assembly of Serbian municipality of Jajce from SPJ. The rest of them refused. Since we had no one to expand it with, the chairman of the local boards who were admitted by virtue of their offices, I asked Mr. Karadzic and you at a counselling in Sarajevo, what was I to do in that case. And then we agreed that the local boards' chairmen enter by virtue of their positions, as it had been arranged, and I was also asked about the number of committee members we planned to have in the Assembly." Mr. Krajisnik, these remarks by the municipality president of Jajce reflect that he acted on the order issued by Dr. Karadzic and you and that he subsequently held a counselling with Dr. Karadzic and you about implementing those instructions.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He saw us - I remember that well - but I assure you that then and today I did not understand this. I would have said to him: You have the recommendation. There was no need for him to rely on any instruction to establish this, especially because he's a minority. And he said here that he did not have enough councilmen. This really comes as a surprise to me, that I would override an Assembly decision and tell someone: Okay, act on some instruction that I don't know about. He probably consulted with us in terms of how they would establish this. The other things he did, when he joined the autonomous region, whatever, I don't know. But I know this president of the municipality came to see us and I know that we talked to him. This was later, when the Serb army liberated Jajce, let me use that vocabulary. But I certainly would have said to him: You have the recommendation. You can establish this. So it was 1993. It wasn't that he talked to me in 1991 or 1992. I just remember 1993 at some point. Oh, I'm so sorry. I don't even know what time it was, but I know that it was when Jajce was liberated that he talked about us how to establish the Assembly. And before that he had annexed whatever, as I see here, with the best of intentions -- I'm so sorry that I have to be giving you all of these no answers. But there was no need for me to say rely on instructions, when there is this recommendation, when there were these legal channels that were there. He talked to me and he talked to him -- well, I believe he did. Maybe he did. But I always had a state document. Why would I need a document that belonged to I don't know who? I never relied on these party documents but only on Assembly decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the time. I think that's probably when the Court wanted to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But perhaps one additional question, Mr. Krajisnik. Do you remember - because I do understand your testimony to be the following - what Mr. -- what the Jajce municipality president says during this session in July, 1993, does not reflect your perception of a meeting you had with him. Why didn't you not at that moment intervene and say: Well, you're referring to a meeting and to instructions, but you must have misunderstood me, you must have misinterpreted what happened because I was not aware that such a thing happens -- happened, what you're now telling us about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, had I known that I would come to The Hague Tribunal, I would have clarified each and every particular matter. The main point was that Jajce was liberated and now he's saying that he's going to establish an Assembly. And two years later he is saying something that doesn't mean a thing to me any longer and I am not going to look at that. Why did I not react to that? Do you know what kind of things people said when they were taking part of the discussion? Why would I deal with something that was said two years earlier on? Before that, Jajce was in the Muslim Croat Federation, and now there was this Assembly and he said that he had founded this Serb Assembly that had stopped functioning at the moment when the war broke out because Jajce was part of the federation throughout the war -- well, throughout the war; all the way to 1993. But this is a new situation and he wants to establish an Assembly. He says: Here I come, a newly liberated territory. Of course I would have reacted if I knew that I would be held accountable and that I'd have to answer for each and every minute detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I'm just looking at the clock. If we would continue until -- at a quarter past 12.00, then we could proceed without any further break, then one and a half hour would remain. That's my suggestion. Yes. We'll adjourn until quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, before we continue, you provided to the Chamber extracts from the 10th of October session to which you referred earlier in your testimony in which you would draw our attention to the words spoken which may have caused you to say what you said at a later stage during that same meeting. We decided that we would give it to the parties because it's part of an explanation. They can look at it - there's no translation yet - with their language assistants and then at whether it's -- is in the interest either of the Defence or the Prosecution to -- to submit this document and to ask for admission into evidence. The Chamber at this moment has not any strong feelings on whether or not to call this. It's not in the core of the case. It seems to explain -- that's at least what you said, it explains why you said certain things. And as you may have noticed this morning, the Chamber -- I couldn't say that the Chamber is not interested in the whys, but the Chamber is primarily interested in the whats rather than the whys, at least on these kind of matters which are not central in this case. So therefore, we leave it to the parties. If it would assist your Defence, Mr. Josse will certainly find a moment to ask for admission. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received this from the OTP, if we are talking about this morning's piece of evidence, the statement of Mr. Filipovic. I just identified the session at which it was made, and I wanted it -- that to be tendered together with the statement of Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll see whether the parties think it's of such importance that it should be tendered if it's not already in evidence. Then, Mr. Josse, did I understand well that you wanted to raise --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, there is something I want to raise. Whilst I do that, Mr. Krajisnik handed to the Chamber yesterday an extract of a statement of Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In fact, it was a speech that he had given at an Assembly session, and in fact there is a -- it's already an exhibit in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which contains that speech or that portion of the speech?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that then, therefore, is to say no statement was given -- at least, Mr. Krajisnik did not -- there was no statement of Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- there is a statement in existence which purportedly comes from Dr. Karadzic which is in the possession of the Defence. That was not -- I think that is on the CD, in fact. Yesterday Mr. Krajisnik handed up a separate document; that, we think, is P69A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll check that and then there's -- at least then there's no need to have it translated again because it's translated already. This clarifies the issue. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to take a point now. I'd be brief about it, and it may be that the Chamber would wish to return to it on another occasion. But as briefly as I can, I wish to object to what has just happened in relation to P1193, the very last document that was put to Mr. Krajisnik. To state the obvious, Variants A and B are an important point in this case. It has been litigated at length by both sides. Mr. Krajisnik's case in relation to that particular document has been clear near enough from the outset of this case. Certainly by the time Mr. Deronjic was cross-examined, it was apparent what Mr. Krajisnik was saying as to his state of knowledge of the Variants A and B document. The Defence question why the Prosecution didn't rely on P1193 as part of their case. The Defence submit that there is an inference the Chamber can draw that the Prosecution have deliberately kept this particular piece of evidence up their sleeve, so to speak, in order to ambush the accused in the course of his evidence. And the cross-examination that the Chamber has just heard in relation to that particular document, we submit, amounts in effect to ambush and is unfair and is prejudicial to the accused. I appreciate that the Prosecution will almost certainly be able to say - and I concede this readily - that that document will have been disclosed. The Chamber is aware of the disclosure process. Many, many documents have been disclosed. The Chamber is well aware that the Defence have not had an opportunity to sort through those documents and assess them in a proper way. But even if that's right, it's not really in issue of disclosure. The question I pose rhetorically is why didn't the Prosecution rely upon that as part of their case, therefore enabling the Defence to answer it properly both in the examination-in-chief of Mr. Krajisnik and also perhaps, I might add, making some inquiries of the author of the statement, the municipal president of Jajce, whose name we don't even know because it's not stated within the Assembly session. Now, as I say, if Your Honour wishes to have this legal argument, so to speak, at some later stage of the case, I have no objection to that. If the Chamber would rather the Defence proceeded by way of motion, we're quite willing to draft and file a motion in relation to this particular matter. I raise it now, one, to preserve my client's position; and two, of course, because I suspect this is going to arise again during the course of the next fortnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is inclined to ask for written submissions on the matter, not necessarily ten pages, but brief written submissions; at the same time, it might assist - and might assist you as well, Mr. Josse - if the Prosecution would like to spend just as little time as you did now in a first response -- well, let's say but at the end of this session or perhaps tomorrow morning the first thing to do. That might give further guidance for you as to what you are -- what you could expect as a response at a later stage. And that could -- might be a good way of keeping the debate within the limits of the necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That would be very helpful, and I'd encourage, too, Your Honour, the Prosecution to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, it's -- I take it that it comes as a surprise at this moment for you, but I'm not urging you to give that very brief response right away. You've seen that Mr. Josse set out the issue in just two or three minutes. If you could set out what will be the basics of your response also in two or three minutes, then on the basis of that we could invite the parties for further written submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that then you will find a suitable moment, today or tomorrow, when to address this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, during the course of the morning's session I had asked you about the -- Dr. Kalinic's remarks and Dr. Karadzic's remarks about Mr. Cizmovic's proposed tour on wheels, remarks made at the Assembly session of February 15th, and I believe I also asked you if you knew to whom Mr. Cizmovic reported. And in connection with those issues, if we could turn next to tab 71. The English at page 30, and the B/C/S at page SA025603 at the bottom, Mr. Krajisnik, and then continuing on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have different numbering. 040 and then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we have no SA0 numbers at the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Maybe -- well, first of all, let me make sure I have enumerated the correct tab. I think we're all looking at tab 71, I believe I said, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, it's 71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I made a mistake. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab 71 contains the transcript from the session of the Deputies Club held on 28 February, 1992, which would be approximately two weeks after the February 15th session we had discussed earlier. These reflect the remarks of Mr. Cizmovic on that date, who says at -- who said at the portion I indicated earlier: "In the end I would like to say that the work with the members of the SDS in Bosnian Krajina" --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You really have to direct me. I cannot follow unless you tell me -- oh, yes, is that at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I indicated, I guess before you were able to actually find the page. At the page of 5603 and then continuing on to 5604.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Cizmovic states: "In the end I would like to say that the work with the members of the SDS in Bosnian Krajina has not been adequate. The work should be intensified, from the deputies to the SDS Main Board here in Sarajevo. And personnel changes are necessary if we want to avoid greater evil. That's what I stated in a study I submitted to the president of the Assembly and the president of the party: My view of Bosnian Krajina and the way to solve it." Now, first of all, Mr. Krajisnik, I take it there's no question that Mr. Cizmovic here is referring to you as the -- when he mentions the president of the Assembly. He means the president of the Assembly of the Serbian People. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he means the president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And by the president of the party he means, of course, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, possibly -- probably. There is no other president of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this appears to be conclusions resulting from the tour on wheels that Mr. Cizmovic was to take, as indicated by Dr. Karadzic on February 15th, 1992, and it appears that he submitted a report about precisely that tour to you and Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really all I see here is that he presented a sort of study about the Bosnian Krajina, and it was probably for the purposes of the president of the party, and maybe he copied it to the president of the Assembly, but it concerns Bosnian Krajina. And if you look at the beginning, it speaks about the SDS and its senior personnel and it goes on to speak about the ultimatum imposed at the Assembly. I don't see that this is a report about some tour; it's just about Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, let's -- let's first of all stick to the facts. Mr. Krajisnik, did you receive such a report or such a study from Mr. Cizmovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember -- like, I never received it. That's what I think. I don't know whether it ever came in. I never read it. Excuse me: I did receive a study from some institute, a vision of Bosnian Krajina, but not from Mr. Cizmovic. The institute concerned is the economical institute, and the study is about what Bosnian Krajina should look like as a region. If that is the study in question, then yes, possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It doesn't look as if Mr. Cizmovic was dealing with these kind of matters. If that report would be available and if it's not in evidence yet, then of course we would have a look at it and see how, on the basis of the date, on the basis of the subject matter, we could see whether this could possibly be the same document as referred to by Mr. Cizmovic. So, you don't remember that you have received it. Do you have any other knowledge? Because if not, then we have to analyse the material we have in front of us if you can't add anything to it. I mean, it's of no use to speculate further on what it could have been, et cetera, apart from such concrete information as could have been this report. Then we'll look at it and otherwise we'll have to deal on the basis of what is in evidence and that is, in this case, the -- for example, among other matters, these minutes in which someone says that he has sent it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can explain right away. I have a newspaper article from the time when the Autonomous Region of Krajina was formed. A feasibility study about Bosnian Krajina was made by this institute, and I remember that I had that kind of paper in my possession. I don't have any other paper. I believe that I can find that newspaper article where you can read about it, but I don't have the study itself with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At first sight, what you describe as what you have received seems not to have the same subject as what this study is supposed to be. But if you want to present it, we'll have a look at it. If it's just a newspaper article, then of course the first thing we are going to do is look at dates and to look at subjects. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I don't know the dates either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to avoid all kind of speculation on what might have been the case. If Mr. Krajisnik doesn't know about it, if he has no memory of it, then again we'll have to do it on the basis of the remainder of the evidence. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I may just clarify, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, is it your testimony that you did not receive a report from Mr. Cizmovic about the inadequacy of the work of the members of the SDS in Bosnian Krajina and the need for personnel changes, or is it your testimony that you don't remember whether or not you received such a report?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember receiving it, but I was aware of those problems; however, I don't remember receiving it. Maybe they copied it to me because it was about the authorities, but Cizmovic did not report to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the words -- the word used by Mr. Cizmovic is "submitted," "I submitted to the president of the Assembly and the president of the party." So the question is whether or not you remember receiving a report submitted by Mr. Cizmovic to you and to Dr. Karadzic concerning the inadequacy of the work of the members of the SDS in Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I received one study concerning the status of the Bosnian Krajina. I remember that. I don't know from whom and from -- and when. But it was made by the economics institute in Banja Luka. Whether that was the study that Cizmovic submitted to Karadzic, me, and maybe somebody else, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to stop you here. That's what you explained before, that it might be another document, and you said that you received that. Now the question is specifically on the report of Mr. Cizmovic. I think your testimony was: If I have received it, it must have been that someone copied it to me. I did not -- it was not directly submitted to me by Mr. Cizmovic, but I do not know. I have no recollection that I saw that, but if I have seen it, then it must have been that someone copied it to me. So that contradicts more or less what was said here that it was submitted to you and not that you received a copy from someone else to whom it was addressed. If this is wrong --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I didn't say "copy." I said if he submitted some sort of material to Mr. Karadzic, he gave the second copy, like, to be handed to Krajisnik. It's not that somebody copied it to -- from Karadzic and gave it to me. He sort of addressed it to both of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The Serbian word for -- is different. It doesn't sound like "copy," but that's what it means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then it's now clear that although you have no recollection that you did receive it, that you do not exclude for the possibility that where it was addressed to Mr. Karadzic, that you were the second one to receive a copy of -- at least, the second one to receive one -- this document as well, and it may even have been addressed to you. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you testified at length, I think it's fair to say, during the course of your examination-in-chief about the -- what you called the Cutileiro agreement and explained its role in or responsibility for or connection to a number of different events and actions. And I'd like to discuss that -- some aspects of that with you now, if I may. And perhaps it's useful for you to have the Sarajevo -- the March 18th, 1992, document in front of you as we do. And that can be found, I believe, at tab 80, which is -- I think it's D5. Now, tab 80 contains D5, "Statement of principles for new constitutional arrangements for Bosnia-Herzegovina." That's the March 18th document we've talked about extensively during the course of your -- well, that you've talked about extensively during the course of your examination-in-chief. Is that right, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have D2 here and D4. I don't know where D5 is. Constituent Units, D; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in the bundle that I have that I think was copied for everyone, tab 80 is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Krajisnik, I understand the confusion. Thank you. Mr. Krajisnik, I was only referring to the exhibit number because that was the exhibit produced. I wasn't asking you to turn to a particular portion of the document yet.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the first issue I wanted to clarify is that this document is -- it is, in fact, something of a misnomer to speak of the Cutileiro agreement, because what emerged from the discussions that concluded on the late evening of March 17th or maybe the early morning hours of March 18th was this document, which was, as it says on the third page of the document, the basis of further negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but look at what it says underneath: "Agreement reached by the leaders of the parties," the SDA and so on. That's why it was called the "Cutileiro agreement." I agree that it is a basis for future negotiations, but it does say down here that agreement was reached. That is why it was called the Cutileiro agreement. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand that. I just -- and how it came to be known in that particular way. I just wanted to clarify because it seemed that there may -- well, I just wanted to clarify that the agreement was that this paper would serve as the basis for further discussions and further negotiations, that there was no agreement to do anything to finalise the issue with respect to Bosnia and Herzegovina; that there was, instead, an agreement about the starting point for the rest of the negotiations, whether or not they would ever come to a final resolution of the dispute.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be quite precise: This is agreement on the foundations on the basis of which we were supposed to continue - how should I put this? - having all of this worked out in detail and reaching a final solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And one of the examples of the fact that it reflected merely the starting point for further discussions that would move wherever they might move rather than some form of final agreement was that there were aspects of it to which you and Dr. Karadzic and the other Bosnian Serb negotiators, as well as the Assembly members, did not agree?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some elements for which we sought improvements, that is to say that the solution was not quite satisfactory, but I agree. Yes, there was an element that we agreed on; that's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One of those elements, for example, was the inclusion in the agreement of -- in the statement of principles that there would be a central bank that -- correct? That was a -- that was an issue to which the Bosnian Serbs were opposed and did not agree.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were different views on the central bank; whether there should be a single currency or not. But that was envisaged here, but we had some reservations with regard to that and so did the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well -- "reservations" might be seen as a mild term. Central -- you were opposed to a central bank.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many questions here that were discussed at these meetings, that is. And what was discussed at the sessions does not imply our opposition. It simply meant that we were seeking improvements. I can tell you how we envisaged the central bank. I can tell you all about it. Just like it is in America, you see. To -- the central bank should have the right of primary issue, for instance. So it's not the problem of the central bank itself. There should be several banks within it that would have the right of issue, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The problem with a central bank - and I'm not particularly worried about the nuances of monetary policy - but the problem with the central bank is that means there is one state and units within that state rather than three individual, sovereign states.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm so sorry, but I did not quite follow what you were saying. Could you just repeat what you said. With the best of intentions, I simply could not manage to follow. Perhaps you put it very well. Perhaps the answer isn't right -- or rather, the question is very good, I'm sure, but could you just repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The fundamental problem with the central bank is that it would mean that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be a single state comprised of three units over which it had control through the monetary policy, rather than a situation in which there were three independent, sovereign units which had control of the important aspects of authority that effectively would make them sovereign. That's the problem with the central bank in a nutshell, isn't it, that concerned the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm an economist. I can tell you exactly the way it was, if you're interested. We wanted to have control over monetary policy, over a joint monetary policy that would be pursued together so that no one would steal from us. That was the problem concerning the central bank. There had to be a currency, no doubt about that, and there was no dispute regarding the existence of a central bank; however, the part that we have, we wanted within our slice of the pie, so to speak, to be able to issue money. And that's exactly what we were looking at, the dollar, that was our example when we were discussing this. It wasn't a problem of whether a central bank would exist, but what kind of control would exist in that central bank; one, two, or three, or altogether, what kind of control would be exercised over monetary policy. And you are right, it is monetary authority, as such, that was a problem, so that no one would steal from anyone. That is quite a big thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You recall earlier in your examination when you were read out - I don't recall specifically whether Mr. Stewart did it, but I know it happened during the course of your examination - your remarks from the February 28th Deputies Club when you said, in effect: We know what they want.
