They want the currency, they want a sovereign BiH, they want the army, but effectively they won't get it. Do you recall those remarks or is it necessary for me to pull out the --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly what I said, exactly. I know exactly why I said it, too. They wanted Yugoslavia; they didn't want to accept these principles, but then I wanted them to accept these principles so we could move on. That's exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those are the attributes of a sovereign, independent state; the army, the currency.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina was supposed to have five or six functions only as a complex state. It was supposed to be either a confederacy or a union or whatever, but it was to be an internationally recognised subject. It was not an ordinary, unitary state. The rest belonged to the constituent units; that is the essence of the whole problem. And we wanted the constituent units to have as much authority as possible and the central authorities as little authority as possible; that's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you and Dr. Karadzic at the session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly that was held on the same date that appears on the statement of principles, March 18th, took pains to assure the deputies that the document had not been signed, was merely a foundation for further negotiations, and did not reflect the fulfilment of the objectives of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that was the policy. On the 11th of March, people refused that plan. So we had to try to represent what was agreed upon as something that was not a unitary Bosnia, that it was, rather, this generally accepted Cutileiro Plan. I know that and that can be seen from here, and it's a different thing that we wanted to prepare them, because they were afraid that this was a unitary Bosnia. They knew what power meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So it's fair to say that all of the deputies understood from you and Dr. Karadzic that the agreement had not been signed. That's correct, that the statement of principles had not been signed; there had been no agreement reached.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The map was the problem, only the map, the one that's attached. On the basis of the map, they were objecting to everything. The map - the Cutileiro map - had certain things involved -- and then we were explaining that we would approve it and this exchange with the Croats, and so on and so forth. There were different meetings in relation to that. The Cutileiro Plan was absolutely accepted as a basis by all the deputies from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say, Mr. Krajisnik, it was not accepted as a basis for moving on. I asked you whether or not all the deputies understood from you and Dr. Karadzic that the statement of principles did not satisfy the objectives of the Bosnian Serbs and that it had not been signed for that reason. That nothing had been signed, nothing was agreed in that way, and that there would be further negotiations. That's all. A. That's certainly what was said, as forcefully as possible; this is the basis, and then we're going to work on that. The map was the problem. Everybody thought it should be different, but basically the principles were unequivocally agreed upon. So you're right, that was a basis for further negotiations, yes. True, it was not signed, but it was agreed upon. People very often confused these things. They say "signed." No, the Cutileiro Plan was not signed; it was agreed upon. And Mr. Cutileiro agreed to it, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look, in that case, at just a couple of portions of that 11th Assembly Session held on March 18th. And let me look first with you at pages 33 through 34 of the English. I'll get to the B/C/S in just a moment, Mr. Krajisnik. And that would be page 46 of the B/C/S, the remarks of Mr. Zekic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 56, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm so sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. If you look quickly at his remarks, you'll see that he's expressing unhappiness with the state of affairs. He begins by talking about the conclusion before, that: "... we should not accept anything less than the confederate option which was reached the last session and was not complied with, and that minimum is where I draw the line." That's in the second paragraph of his remarks. We -- the fourth paragraph: "We claim all the time that we will take action and do something." And then he continues to express his dissatisfaction and says: "All negotiations will continue, and Bosnia-Herzegovina will exist as an internationally recognised entity that will keep postponing to deal with internal arrangements for a decade. The arrangement will never happen, and with their birth rate they will gradually stifle our territories too ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if you think that the interpreters can follow you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "... and we shall find ourselves in a difficult situation. "I do not think that anything can be accomplished without a clearly defined Serbian state, a separate state that can sign treaties on confederation with anybody. We cannot accept anything less and I can cannot accept anything less. I shall never sign anything else, and I shall distance myself from all this." And then you speak, Mr. Krajisnik saying: "What can I say after hearing Zekic. As if we had not discussed anything, as if he had just now entered the room! "Did we not say that nothing was agreed as yet, that this was working material. Did we not say that one basic principle was established, but this principle was not included in the material in its final form: That Bosnia and Herzegovina was divided into three parts. What they are going to be called, remains to be discussed next." And then you continue in the next long paragraph: "We have stated that the three parts should be states. They objected to calling them states at this point, but we insisted that they should be called states. Our work is not yet finished, gentlemen. This is just one phase. If we cannot achieve our goal and carry out the mandate we received from this Assembly, then we will do whatever is necessary to protect our interests. No one has the right to agree to anything without the consent of this Assembly." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, that would indicate that the disagreement with the statement of principles went to issues beyond the maps, went to some -- to one of the fundamental, if not the fundamental, aspect of the statement of principles. Isn't that what Mr. Zekic is talking about and isn't that what you're reassuring him will be addressed at a later stage? And if it can't be addressed satisfactory, then the Bosnian Serbs will do whatever is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This shows that Mr. Zekic is an exception. I'm saying that it's as if he just walked in through the door. My first sentence is that. So this is not the view of the Assembly; this is the view of Mr. Zekic. There were different proposals. You're right. At this session there was one basic problem: People wanted to remain in Yugoslavia and they kept going back to that. Here we were supposed to adopt Bosnia as a state with three constituent units, and we adopted that. Truth to tell, it was hard and painstaking. You see that Zekic said: I'm never going to sign this, as if he were to sign it. But he's a deputy, he wants to stay in Yugoslavia, he doesn't want to be a minority, and so on. It's very dangerous if one expounds this view that we did not accept these principles. We adopted these principles at -- one more thing, I'm sorry, Mr. Prosecutor. Even apart from these principles, we had agreed on a great many things but they could not fit into the principles. A lot was already clear as to what would be done in the future. Our course had been charted at this meeting with Mr. Cutileiro. And that is why he said that there was a statement -- rather, that when we reach agreement we have a referendum, all three parties adopt it, and then we adopt a constitution. There is a statement that says that. I can give you -- I can bring it here, a copy of the newspapers stating what he said. It's best to hear about it from him directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, are you suggesting that you were prepared to accept statement of principles as a final document that made -- that put the Bosnian Serbs in a unit within an independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were, Mr. Prosecutor, but you will find hundreds of statements after that where we said "our state," and so on and so forth. That is politics, how all of this can get through so that we move on, because people kept saying we want to have our own state, we don't want to leave Yugoslavia. They kept repeating that five years afterwards. But we accepted the agreement: We're giving up on Yugoslavia, but we do want Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is incontrovertible. It's different when you have these belligerent statements that you're trying to find ways and means of explaining this. Look at this here. You see it says state. We mentioned that Bavaria is a state, that Texas is a state and so on. And we said, well, don't call it a state, it's not the right time for that. Call it whatever you want. But people like calling it a state although it's a constituent unit, but within Bosnia-Herzegovina. Not as a state but as a composite state community. That was the agreement reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you say I'll find hundreds of statements, am I also going to find many statements in which you and Dr. Karadzic insist that you will never accept a situation where the Bosnian Serbs are within a unitary or independent Bosnia and never accept a situation in which -- where the Bosnian Serbs cannot be in a joint state with Serbia and other Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you will find several statements where we said that we would never be in a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is correct. Later on, the translation was poor. Very often it was stated that we would not be separated from Serbia, and this was a reference to special ties. Now it's different how this is interpreted at the session itself, but people did not want to have a border on the Drina and not to have passports. And that is what we achieved through special ties, between Serbia and Republika Srpska, and Croatia and everybody else. And I showed you that, what Mr. Izetbegovic said. He agreed. Everybody agreed that we had the right to special ties in exchange for a state. With Yugoslavia, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, maybe I can short-circuit some of this by seeking your position on it. You stated: "Very often it was stated that we would not be separated from Serbia, and this was a reference to special ties." Is it necessary for me to collect and show you statements by you and Dr. Karadzic beginning in 1991 and extending on through 1992, 1993, 1994, assuring the representatives of the Bosnian Serb people that you would never accept a situation that -- in which Republika Srpska or the Bosnian Serb people were not living in a sovereign state of Bosnian Serbs and in which you could not form a united state - whether it was an alliance of states or a single state - with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'll give you all the plans that I took part in, and that is what counts. In every plan we accepted Bosnia as a state. And now you're talking about statements. Yes, you're right. There's hundreds of statements for political purposes when the Muslims were rejecting the plan, and then we opted for negotiations. And we were trying to overcome what somebody had undermined for us. We worked on this for three months and then it went down the drain. And then another one for years and months, and it went down the drain. We accepted all of them except for the Vance-Owen Plan. It is true that this was a discussion. Yes, that is what I said in the discussion, too, but that was talk. But tell me, was there a single plan where we did not accept Bosnia as a state except for the Vance Plan, which was abolishing Republika Srpska? But we accepted all of this. Also, at rallies I spoke. Yes, that's correct, in order to win an election and so on and so forth. But please, our position was in the plan and in the plan we said that Bosnia is a state. And we reached agreement on that with Mr. Cutileiro straight away, and we kept referring to the Cutileiro principles. There's not a single plan where we did not refer to those principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you're suggesting to the Court, Mr. Krajisnik, that in order to determine your state of mind, it should focus only on the results of the negotiations in which you participated, rather than the -- than the many, many statements about those issues that exist to the contrary? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct. Because statements were made for political purposes just in order to continue the negotiations. And each of my statements was made in times of crisis when somebody disrupted the negotiations, not because we wouldn't accept Bosnia as a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, just like you said on March 18th, 1992, to the representatives of the Assembly about the statement of principles that had been reached in the Cutileiro negotiations, your involvement in the negotiations thereafter represented attempts to reach a long-term objective step by step, taking what you could at any given point and moving forward from there. That's the reality of it, isn't it, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in order for something to succeed at a given Assembly session, you tell people: Come on, accept this, but we are moving on to achieve our goals. You have to do that if you want to sell something. If you don't want to sell anything, then you say: Okay, this is final and we all go home, and then we end up guilty because we didn't accept the Cutileiro Plan. No. We said we accept the principles, we give up on the idea of Yugoslavia, and we move on. That's the road we took all the time, throughout those years. It's only when somebody abandoned these principles that we rebelled and opposed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you repeatedly told the Bosnian Serb people what those goals were and reminded the deputies that the compromise positions that were then available in negotiations were merely steps on the way to that ultimate goal?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our ultimate goal was what we could achieve at negotiations. And when the possibility emerged, when somebody offered us this declaration to sign to announce the referendum and to leave, Izetbegovic signed it and I signed it, too, because every Serb wanted to unite with Serbia, but that was not realistic. And I said: Our goal is what is feasible at negotiations. Our goal could not be something that is unacceptable to the other side. That's why I put this in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will likely be returning to this but not -- because of the time I want to move on to one other very closely related subject that you mentioned. You also indicated, of course, that the problem with the Cutileiro agreement or negotiations or whatever we'll call it on March 18th was the maps. And we spent a great deal of time in your examination-in-chief talking about maps, as the Court and you will, no doubt, recall. First of all, if I could turn your attention to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, Mr. Krajisnik. I'm trying to retrieve the document that Mr. Krajisnik produced at the conclusion of the examination-in-chief. Your Honour, I believe this document -- this is a -- reflects a portion of D247.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, if you look at the last page of --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's best to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From what I understood, it was just the maps that were brought to our attention, the other parts of the document being cut off as being irrelevant, but I now take it that when it should receive a new number because this is the text now becoming part of the evidence as well, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar -- yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, these maps are even better than the ones I provided. They are much more legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's partly why we did that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I do see that you translated portions of the text as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, the new number would be -- would be P --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1194, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1194, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krajisnik, looking at P1194, although I think you essentially answered this question in your comments a moment ago, the -- it contains the -- the full article of -- that was represented by the partial portion of that newspaper article that you provided in D247.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as you --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the whole page. I believe that's one whole page of the Politika newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And as you indicated, we see there the three maps representing the proposals of the three parties and -- which I understand to be the Serb map on top, the Muslim map in the middle, and the Croat at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to tab 83 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just check one matter very quickly, Your Honour. We have sent the maps in P1194 themselves to the CLSS for translation. Does the Court still require the maps themselves to be translated, as opposed to the text? I'm not altogether clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that this new document contains the -- all the written text, including -- all the written text attached to the maps. I suggest that a note will be made on D -- what is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 247, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 247, that a note will be made, which I will initial, on D247 that the translation is found at P1193.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll inform CLSS not to proceed with that translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Now we are at D7B, the map under tab 83.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, looking at D7B, the map behind tab 83, Mr. Krajisnik, that appears to be a fourth map. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's Cutileiro's map. So none of those that you gave me. This is Cutileiro's map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you say "Cutileiro's map," what do you mean by that; that Mr. Cutileiro submitted this map as a fourth person in the negotiations or a fourth party in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. When we proposed those three maps, then Mr. Darwin tabled his map as a sort of compromise. So that's that last map attached to the principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You're saying this map, D7B behind tab 83, is a map that was attached to the principles and submitted by Mr. Darwin?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Darwin, who was an associate of Mr. Cutileiro, and that was attached to the principles at our Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what do you mean attached to the principles at your Assembly session? Maybe it's a bad translation. What Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were discussing on the 18th, was it? February or March. When we discussed these principles, then this map was attached to the principles and it was the map discussed, not the three earlier ones. It was a general map identifying territories that would be Muslim, Croat, and Serb respectively, with Sarajevo as an extraterritorial location. Not all of it, but it was supposed to be under the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well -- and this issue came up during the course of the Prosecution case. If you look at tab 82, D7. That was a map -- or that is a map, as we indicated to the Court and to you and your counsel, Mr. Krajisnik, during the course of the Prosecution's case, that was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by Mr. Cutileiro, which appears to reflect the municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, indicating essentially where there were the different groups have an absolute or relative majority.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, Mr. Prosecutor. This is the Muslim map. Look at it. It's the same as this other map, and look at the title where Cutileiro says that Sarajevo would be ex-territorial, whereas on this map Sarajevo is not separate. Everything is, instead, divided between three territorial units. This is the Muslim map. Look at it; it's the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, why don't we look, instead, to the statement of principles themselves at tab 80, and in particular, on the third page of that document, "Definition of the Constituent Units."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Under (E), as I indicated, it states: "A working group will be established in order to define the territory of the constituent units based on national principles and taking into account economic, geographical, and other criteria. A map based on the national absolute or relative majority in each municipality will be the basis of work in the working group and will be subject only to amendments justified by the above-mentioned criteria. A copy is annexed to this statement."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. And that is the map that you saw the first time. Not the one that you've just shown but the map that we saw first. I don't know at which tab it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You've got two tabs --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps confusing at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You've got two tabs; tab 82 and 83. 82 appears to represent a map in which the municipalities are shaded in according -- consistent with the absolute or relative majorities, and 83 appears to be a map which is based, to say the least, on a different principle and does not appear to identify the territory by municipality. Which of those two maps is it you say was annexed to the statement of principles?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance. You have in your material here at the beginning exactly what Cutileiro said about Sarajevo. Your first map is the Muslim map. It does not show Sarajevo. And he told me to read this and you will translate it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it's a simple question. We have the map in Latin writing, more or less handwriting, and we have the one in Cyrillic we find under tab 83. Which of these maps was attached to the statement of principles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D7B is Cutileiro's map, and that was attached to the principles. Whatever somebody may have written before, it's that map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No -- you say it was the map that we find under tab 83 that is in Cyrillic with typewritten text. That was the map, and not 82 that was attached to the statement of principles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This map -- it's probably copied from somewhere, I don't know. But that -- this is the map that was attached to Cutileiro principles. Yes, it's true, it's written in Cyrillic. It must have been copied from some document, but this kind of map was attached, whereas the other map, written in Latinic script, is the Muslim map. And here it is in the newspaper, the same map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Tieger, is that at least clear, I hope?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I think the answer is clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, among other things, Mr. Krajisnik, are you saying that the map submitted by Cutileiro -- well, as you -- let me correct that. You've been talking about D7B for quite a while and indicating that it was based on settlements and not on municipalities. Do I have that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map was made as a compromise in order to form three constituent units, and it's natural that he marked Muslims, Croat, and Serb majority territories as a basis for discussion. You see, there is no corridor drawn on this map anywhere. Mr. Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But please, let me help you. Just to avoid confusion. I hope you're interested in the truth. It says here: Sarajevo will be extraterritorial with Serb parts, whereas in the other map there is no separate Sarajevo. It says at the beginning: All of Bosnia in three parts. It's another matter that this format was copied from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the format. I was focussed on the issue of municipalities, so please listen to my questions and we'll get to the truth that much faster, I hope. I -- the map that you have been referring to, D7B, at tab 83, I think you made some effort to tell us is -- is different from the Muslim map, perhaps in a number of ways, but certainly in that the map submitted by the Muslim side was based on municipalities and this map, D7B, was based on settlements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I foresee that we get a similar -- similar confusion, both on the basis of the earlier testimony and on the maps itself. Is the difference, Mr. Krajisnik, between the two maps that the one reflects only what is a majority -- or a majority municipality, whereas the map in tab 83 also took into consideration, although not consistently in every detail, but also took into consideration majorities in smaller units - villages, et cetera - and was not exclusively based upon majority population and municipalities? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. It took it into consideration roughly. Not municipalities but some sort of units in order to round off the entities, whereas the Muslims did take it into account in their own way. That is -- was their proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Does that answer the question, Mr. Tieger, you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, we've already looked at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said "please proceed," but at the same time, looking at the clock, I notice it's a quarter to 2.00. Therefore, we have to adjourn for the day. We adjourn for the day, but not until after I have reminded -- have instructed you, Mr. Krajisnik, that you should not speak to anyone about the testimony you have given or you're still about to give. And we adjourn until tomorrow, 9.00, in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 2nd day of June, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
